name: Cow urine (gomutra)

card.summary: Gomutra, cow urine used in Ayurveda and Hindu practice, applied or taken by some with the hope of clearer skin and better general health.
card.aka: Gomutra, gaumutra, cow's urine arka, panchagavya component
card.note: Drinking or applying animal urine can carry infection risk, and an acute urticaria case has been reported after gomutra gargles.

quick.overview:
Gomutra is the urine of the cow, regarded as sacred in Hinduism and used for centuries in Ayurvedic medicine, often within the five-product mixture called panchagavya. It is sold in India as a drink, in distilled form (arka), and as an ingredient in soaps, face packs and skin preparations.

For appearance, supporters use it for skin concerns and general cleansing, reasoning that its reported antimicrobial properties help with skin and hair complaints. Laboratory reviews describe antimicrobial activity, but the claims about curing disease are not backed by robust clinical trials, according to reference sources.
quick.how: Practitioners take gomutra as a drink or distilled arka, and it also appears as an ingredient in soaps, creams and washes, or is used diluted on the skin. It is commonly paired with other cow products in panchagavya preparations.
quick.risks: Raw cow urine can carry animal-borne bacteria such as E. coli, and gomutra gargles have been reported to cause acute urticaria. A traditional cow urine concoction containing tobacco and other plant ingredients has been linked to child deaths in Nigeria. People with immune suppression or on medicines should discuss any use with a clinician.

lead: Gomutra (cow urine) is a traditional Indian remedy and ritual substance. It is sacred in Hinduism, features in the ritual mixture panchagavya, and has long been used in Ayurvedic medicine, including as a drink and as an ingredient in topical preparations [1][2].

The route to better looks is through skin and hair care. Proponents describe it as a cleanser and skin remedy, and commercial products include soaps, washes and distilled arka that mention cow urine. A review in an ethnopharmacology journal reports antimicrobial activity in laboratory studies against a range of bacteria, which advocates cite as a reason for its use on skin [3].

Reference sources say the broader claims that it cures diseases are not backed by robust clinical trials, and public-health bodies and clinicians have noted infection risks [2]. Its use became politically prominent in India in 2015 and during the COVID-19 pandemic [2].

chain: Gomutra or arka applied or taken
Antimicrobial and cleansing action (reported in laboratory work)
Fewer skin and scalp complaints (as claimed)
angle.text: Users apply gomutra-based soaps and washes, or take it by mouth, hoping to improve skin and general health. Laboratory reviews report antimicrobial activity, but its effect on complexion has not been measured in controlled trials.

paras: Gomutra is used as a drink, in distilled form, and as a component of panchagavya, the mixture of five cow products used in Hindu ritual and Ayurvedic preparations [2][4]. A 2015 review in the Journal of Intercultural Ethnopharmacology describes the Indian tradition that places the Bos indicus cow at the centre of many remedies [3]. Case reports from Ayurvedic practitioners describe panchagavya formulations in wound and palliative care [5].
Appearance uses sit alongside these medical uses: cow urine appears in soaps, washes and skin preparations marketed as natural cleansers.

Reference sources describe a long Ayurvedic role. Medical anthropologist Joseph Alter has argued that modern Indian urine-therapy practice resembles the approach popularised in the early twentieth century by British naturopath John W. Armstrong more than traditional Ayurveda [2]. A cow-urine refinery opened in Jalore, Rajasthan, in May 2015, and a cow-urine floor cleaner was proposed for government offices that year [2]. In March 2020 a Hindu Mahasabha event in India invited attendees to drink cow urine to ward off COVID-19; health authorities and scientists said no evidence supported this, and in 2021 two men were detained in Manipur over statements that cow urine and dung do not cure COVID-19 before courts ordered their release [2].

Reviews of the laboratory literature describe antimicrobial activity of cow urine against bacteria, in some studies compared with standard antibiotics, and discuss its chemical composition [3][6]. Reviews of cow products note that composition varies with the region and the animal's diet [6].

No studies found examining cow urine for skin appearance. A 2026 exploratory randomised open-label trial in India studied a Triphala vaginal douche with and without a gomutra distillate in vaginal candidiasis, which concerns a different condition [7]. Published human reports on cow-urine products are mostly case reports of Ayurvedic care [5].

Consuming cow urine or dung can transmit animal-borne bacteria such as E. coli, according to reference sources [2]. A case report described acute urticaria after gargling with gomutra [8]. A review of a traditional cow urine concoction in Nigeria, which also contained tobacco, garlic, basil and other ingredients, linked it to respiratory depression and deaths in children treated for convulsions, with nicotine among the main compounds identified [9].

timeline.event: John W. Armstrong popularises urine therapy in the West [2].
Cow-urine refinery opens in Jalore, Rajasthan; Ayurveda reviews of its antimicrobial potential published [2][3].
Cow-urine drinking event in India held to ward off COVID-19 [2].
